chapter: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
title: Coleman Hawkins and the shift from fast dance tempos to slow playing
summary: He calls Hawkins the greatest saxophonist, describes sitting beside him and watching him develop, and explains that ballroom bands played fast until Hawkins brought slow playing.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: What about saxophone players of that period, the '20s? I guess Coleman Hawkins had quite an impact.

Oh, yes, yes, yes. Well, that was a great thing. Coleman Hawkins was one of the greatest. He was one of the greatest saxophone players because he had such a conception of playing the horn and he was a thorough musician, because he could play all the chords. He knew all the chords, you know, because you can tell just listening to him he played

more actually than anybody else. Of course people have come along since then, but to my mind he did it all. Coleman Hawkins did it all. And it's very interesting to listen to him and his whole career, like the old records he made with Fletcher Henderson, way back when Fletcher first started, which was '23 and '24 and '25, to see Coleman develop, develop as he went along and got older, and it was very enlightening to sit in the same section with him and see him develop like that, you know. Yeah, very -- it was very—and I remember when he started -- you see, before that the accent was on dancing, like I said before, and in dancing at that time all dance s were fast. People used to dance fast in those days, you know. Except if you went to a house rent party and they'd have what they called a slow drag, which is different, you know. You like to put your arms around a girl, you know, and -- but in the ballrooms -- in the ballrooms, they were used to playing fast. They had dances called the Balquinade(?)and the One-Step. They were quick, you know. So naturally the bands concentrated on playing fast, fast music. So then there weren't too many saxophone players who were gaited to playing slow music, you know, and Coleman was one of the first who started playing the slow type of music, and I remember one day he told me -- I wasn't with Fletcher then. I'd been away somewhere. I think I was playing with Kirby. He says, "Uh-huh, now you'll learn how to play slow." Just the opposite, you'd think that you'd

learn to play slow then to play fast, but the concentration was on playing fast, like, "Tiger Rag," you know, fast. (Singing). Like that, you know. And the clarinet players were in. The clarinet players -- it's not like now. You don't find clarinet players now.
